content.text:
The drawing shows a central carbon carrying an H, an OH, a phenyl group (Ph), and a group labeled "PH3C".

"PH3C" is most likely a misprint of H3C, which would make the molecule 1-phenylethanol. Read literally, though, "PH3C" means a carbon bearing a PH3 group, i.e. a phosphonium-like or phosphorane-type substituent. Written out, that is a CH2 attached to PH3, so the drawing could be read as PH3-CH2-CH(OH)Ph. The label is probably the pre-formatted "H3C" with a stray "P", but the instruction is to read the structure from the drawing itself.

Taking the label literally, "PH3C" is a carbon with a PH3 attached. The carbon would then be bonded to P, to the central CH, and to H atoms. With P as PH3 (neutral, a phosphine) and the carbon needing four bonds, the substituent is P–CH2–: the P is bonded to C, and the label gives it 3 H.

This gives the literal SMILES for PH3 bonded to CH2, which is a pentavalent phosphorane-like P: PH3(CH2...) → P(H)(H)(H)CC(O)c1ccccc1. Only the P–C bond is drawn, so phosphorus carries 3 H plus 1 C, which is four bonds, and the SMILES would be written with explicit hydrogens as [PH3]. In SMILES, writing P with its implied hydrogens would give PH3 only for valence 3, so I would write [PH3] explicitly. The carbon attached to P is then CH2, so the SMILES is [PH3]CC(O)c1ccccc1.

SMILES: [PH3]CC(O)c1ccccc1
